latest_release.body:
**Before upgrading.** No migrations run in this release: the database stays at
`0088_approval_reviewer_guidance`, and a 1.0.1 database is used as it is. Upgrading from 1.0.0 or
0.3.x runs the migrations listed under 1.0.1, and a database that has run them does not go back:
restore the backup taken before the upgrade instead. Three things change for an existing OpenBot
Desktop installation:
- On Windows OpenBot now always runs in a Podman machine of its own, `openbot`, beside any of
  yours, and on a Mac it does when yours is rootless, after asking to pause it (below). An
  installation that ran in a machine of yours starts fresh in `openbot`, and its earlier data stays
  in your machine.
- At setup and at every Start, a Docker Desktop or Podman too old to run OpenBot is updated
  (below). Docker Desktop quits while it updates, which stops its containers; the ones that were
  running are started again afterwards.
- OpenBot Desktop's back end and the Helm chart move to CopilotKit Intelligence 0.16.0-rc.11, and
  the bundled CLI to `copilotkit@7bd073b` (below).

### OpenBot Desktop

- **Installing a new OpenBot over the old one on Windows never offers to delete your data, and
  uninstalling stops what OpenBot runs.** Running a new installer over an installed OpenBot opened
  the old version's uninstaller in the middle of the update, with a "Delete the application data"
  box, and one wrong tick deleted your Bots and conversations. The old version is now removed
  silently, as an update, on the Installing page, which says "Removing the previous version of
  OpenBot. Your Bots and data stay." with its progress bar moving. If OpenBot is open, the installer
  asks before it closes it. Uninstalling from Settings > Apps used to close OpenBot and leave its
  containers, its services and its Podman machine (`openbot`) running. It now stops them first,
  with the same Compose OpenBot runs, and never touches your own Podman machines or containers.
  Tick "Delete the application data" to remove OpenBot's machine, the backend OpenBot created and
  OpenBot's files in its installation folder as well, so installing again starts from nothing; a
  file of yours in that folder stays. Otherwise they stay, stopped, for a reinstall to find. And on
  Windows, an OpenBot whose own Podman machine is gone makes it again when it opens. It used to open
  on "OpenBot can't run on this computer as it's set up", having looked at your own machine.
- **Setup says what self-contained means up front, and asks about usage data last.** The first
  screen, "Set up OpenBot (self-contained)", says this version runs entirely on your computer,
  backend included, that setup takes between 1 and 10 minutes depending on your internet speed,
  and that in production OpenBot for Business runs on your own infrastructure with Kubernetes, or on
  OpenBot Cloud, with a link to book a demo. The usage-data notice moved off
  it to the foot of the last screen, Finishing setup, as a small checkbox, checked by default as
  before: it is the same setting as Settings > General > Privacy > Share usage data. The Account
  step's heading is now "Get your free license key".
- **OpenBot uses its own Podman machine when yours can't run it, and leaves yours as it is.** A
  Podman machine made with `podman machine init` is rootless, and OpenBot used it and stopped at
  "Change this computer's setup" because local Intelligence needs rootful Podman. On Windows even a
  rootful machine of yours left chat unable to reach OpenBot's back end. OpenBot now makes and uses
  its own rootful machine, `openbot`, as on a computer with none. On Windows it runs beside yours,
  which keeps running untouched, and never takes Docker's default pipe (`docker_engine`), so your
  Docker tools and Docker Desktop keep reaching what they did. On a Mac, where Podman runs one
  machine at a time, OpenBot asks before it pauses your rootless machine while it runs (**Pause my
  Podman**), and Quit starts yours again with

# OpenBot ### AI coworkers. Ready for the enterprise. A modular, self-hostable workspace for AI coworkers.
Choose your models. Bring your agents. Own your infrastructure. [open.bot](https://open.bot) · [Docs](docs/README.md) · [Deploy on Kubernetes](#deploy-on-kubernetes) · [Run from source](#run-from-source) [![GitHub Trending: #3 Repository Of The Day](https://trendshift.io/api/badge/repositories/175080)](https://trendshift.io/repositories/175080) [![Trendshift: #3 Repository Of The Day](https://trendshift.io/api/badge/trendshift/repositories/175080/daily)](https://trendshift.io/repositories/175080)

[![OpenBot for Business: get early access](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenBot_for_Business-Get_early_access_%E2%86%92-D14B9C?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=3A3466)](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=business&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) From [CopilotKit](https://www.copilotkit.ai), creators of [AG-UI](https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui).
https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c60f07da-8b6d-46eb-a573-17fc1e65a644

Watch a Bot use its browser and tools, answer with interactive results, and wait for your approval before it sends. Take over when it needs you, and connect the agents you already run.

## Getting started ### On your laptop The easiest way to get started is with the fully self-contained app that runs on your laptop, combining the OpenBot frontend and Docker-based backend in one application. [Mac / Apple silicon](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-mac-arm64.dmg) · [Mac / Intel](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-mac-x64.dmg) · [Windows](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-windows-x64-setup.exe) [Run from source](#run-from-source) ### For your team **OpenBot for Business** brings your agents into one workspace with company sign-in, tool permissions, approvals, and audit. Deploy on your infrastructure or work with our engineers on hosting and customization. [**Get early access to OpenBot for Business →**](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=business&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [**Talk to an engineer**](https://open.bot/business) · [**Kubernetes setup**](#deploy-on-kubernetes) ### Web, mobile, and chat [Web](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=web&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [iOS](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=ios&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [Android](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=android&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [Slack](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=slack&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [Teams](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=teams&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) ## Your workspace. Your stack.
- **Choose your models.** Use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, or open models through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, hosted by a provider or on your own infrastructure. Keep your provider relationships and change models as your needs change. - **Bring your agents.** Run built-in Bots in the OpenBot server, or connect your existing agents through AG-UI from any agent execution platform. Agents built with different stacks can work in the same workspace. - **Make it yours.** Use the MIT-licensed template as-is, white-label it, or customize it deeply. AG-UI connects agents, MCP connects tools, and the frontends and backend can evolve independently. - **Govern work across your team.** Company sign-in, roles, tool permissions, approvals, and audit apply across the workspace. Your agents use OpenBot's tools and computers under the same policies. - **Get help deploying it.** CopilotKit's engineers can work with your team to deploy OpenBot, connect your systems, and automate parts of specific jobs. [Connect your agent](#bring-your-own-agent) · [Configure models and tools](docs/configuration.md) · [Explore OpenBot for Business](https://open.bot/business) ## Built on CopilotKit and AG-UI OpenBot is built on [CopilotKit](https://www.copilotkit.ai), which is [used in production by a majority of Fortune 500 companies](https://www.copilotkit.ai/blog/series-a). **Your agent stack.** [AG-UI](https://docs.ag-ui.com/introduction#supported-integrations) has first-class integrations across the major agent frameworks and harnesses, including Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework and Agent Harness, Google ADK, AWS Strands, Oracle Agent Spec, LangChain, Mastra, Pydantic AI, Agno, and CrewAI. Many ship first-party support; [Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supports AG-UI directly](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-agui.html). **Your execution platform.** Keep your agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Managed Agents, [Google's Agent Platform](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform), LangChain's Managed Deep Agents, [Microsoft Foundry Agent Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/hosted-agents), or your own infrastructure. Connect them to OpenBot through an AG-UI endpoint, using an adapter where needed. Your choice of agent platform stays independent of your workspace. ## Architecture OpenBot has three parts. On your laptop, setup runs the backend and Intelligence for you. For a team, the Helm chart deploys both on Kubernetes in your own infrastructure. | Part | What it does | | --- | --- | | **OpenBot frontends** | Mac, Windows, web, iOS, Android, Slack, and Teams connect people to the same workspace. Conversations, interactive results, computer view, and approvals adapt to each surface. [Choose a frontend](#getting-started). | | **OpenBot backend** | Runs the workspace API and built-in Bots, connects external agents and tools, manages Bot computers, and enforces identity, permissions, action policies, and audit. Deploys on Kubernetes with PostgreSQL and persistent storage. | | **CopilotKit Intelligence** | Durable conversations, memory, Automatic Learning, and enterprise governance services. Separately licensed; runs on Kubernetes alongside OpenBot. | OpenBot enforces sign-in, tool permissions, action policies, and audit at its API, alongside Intelligence's platform services. Built-in Bots run in the OpenBot server; your own agents can run alongside OpenBot or on any agent execution platform. Both use AG-UI and can share the same workspace. Computer execution is pluggable: use the default Kubernetes setup or connect a compatible external computer provider. [Architecture details](docs/architecture.md) · [Services and ports](#services-and-ports) · [Kubernetes deployment](#deploy-on-kubernetes) ## Open source, local operation, and licensing **The OpenBot application template is open source under the [MIT license](LICENSE).** You can fork, modify, and white-label it. It uses **CopilotKit Intelligence**, which is separately licensed and can run entirely on your own machine or infrastructure. | Where you run it | CopilotKit Intelligence license | | --- | --- | | **Your laptop, for personal use and experimentation** | Requires a free local Intelligence license. Desktop setup handles this for you. | | **Kubernetes evaluation** | Requires a free Intelligence trial license. [Request a trial](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=business&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access). | | **Kubernetes / production** | Requires a production Intelligence license beyond evaluation. OpenBot for Business includes Intelligence for use with OpenBot. [Plans and pricing](https://open.bot/pricing). | **Fully local is an option.** Run OpenBot, Intelligence, and a compatible model locally. A cloud model or connected online app still sends requests to that service. Initial downloads, account sign-in, and local license renewal need internet access. --- ## Deploy on Kubernetes Deploy OpenBot and CopilotKit Intelligence together on **AWS EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE, or your own Kubernetes cluster**. The chart installs Intelligence by default; no separate hosted project is required. For a first evaluation, you need a cluster with **amd64 nodes**, a **default StorageClass**, `kubectl`, Helm, a **trial or production license**, and a model key. The commands below use an OpenAI key. For Anthropic, a model router, cluster sizing, or an existing Intelligence deployment, use the full Helm guide that comes with the chart (`helm show readme` on the chart below). > **Setting up with an AI assistant?** Give it this README and the Helm guide (`helm show readme` on the chart below). The guide covers cloud-specific values, storage, secrets, sign-in, networking, upgrades, and troubleshooting. Use the evaluation below only through a local port-forward; configure sign-in and TLS before sharing a deployment. 1. **Create `openbot-values.yaml` locally.** Replace the placeholders with your license and model key. Keep this file out of source control. ```yaml config: singleUser: true postgresql: enabled: true secrets: licenseToken: "" modelApiKey: "" ``` 2. **Install** the chart published with the release. ```sh helm install openbot https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot/releases/download/v1.0.2/openbot-0.2.0.tgz \ --namespace openbot --create-namespace \ --values openbot-values.yaml \ --timeout 15m ``` 3. **Open your evaluation.** ```sh kubectl -n openbot get pods,jobs kubectl -n openbot port-forward svc/openbot-server 3001:3001 ``` Open . This configuration is single-user: anyone who can reach it is an administrator. Keep the port-forward local. The chart creates the runtime credentials, installs the databases, bootstraps Intelligence, and sets up the Learning container and scheduled jobs. Automatic Learning uses your model key too. For a team deployment, follow the Helm guide (`helm show readme` on the chart) to configure authentication, TLS, your database, secrets, persistent storage, and network policies. For a single-container alternative, see [Deploy it](#deploy-it). ## Run from source Use the template to customize the workspace, branding, Bots, and skills. The source setup below uses managed Intelligence by default; [local Intelligence](#intelligence-on-your-own-machine) is also available. ```sh git clone https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot.git cd OpenBot ``` ### Requirements To run the open-source template locally, you’ll need the following. - Docker, for PostgreSQL, the API server and the shipped Bots. The server, its routine worker and the Bots' computers run from the published OpenBot images, which `scripts/start.sh` pulls at the tag in `backend-images.env`: `main` in a checkout of `main`, the images built from main, and the release's own version in a release (`v1.0.3` in the v1.0.3 tag). Nothing else is built or needed for them. - [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.4+, for the app, the setup helpers and the tests (some tests fail on 1.3). - A CopilotKit Intelligence project and license. A free plan is available, and Intelligence can be self-hosted. - A model key. The proof-of-concept Bot uses OpenAI; the LangGraph Bot can use OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google. ### Quick start The example configuration sets `OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true`, so you can try the app as a local administrator. Configure [sign-in](#sign-in) before giving anyone else access. On a Mac, the free Developer plan also covers [running Intelligence locally](#intelligence-on-your-own-machine) with Docker. > **Setting up with an AI assistant?** Paste [`prompt.txt`](prompt.txt) into it first. It carries the > same steps as below plus the things that are easy to get wrong: which of the blank keys in > `.env.example` are actually yours to fill (the CopilotKit key and a model key), which the start > script fills for you, and what each start-up refusal means. Every claim in it is checked against > this repository. 1. Create `.env`: ```sh cp .env.example .env bun install ``` 2. Connect a fresh managed Intelligence project: ```sh npx --yes copilotkit@latest login npx --yes copilotkit@latest project select bun scripts/setup-learning.ts ``` The helper provisions the selected project's runtime key, creates or reuses its `openbot` Learning container, then writes both settings to `.env`. It preserves custom container assignments and never replaces an existing OpenBot key; with one set, it only creates `openbot` in that key's project if it is missing. For fresh self-hosted setup, set `INTELLIGENCE_API_URL` to that deployment's HTTPS API origin (or `http://localhost` for a local one) and run the helper without the two `npx` commands. It opens an isolated Chrome or Edge window for your usual sign-in and project choice; install either browser first. For CLI-managed local evaluation installs, it discovers the matching dashboard with the newest installed or cached CopilotKit CLI and uses that dashboard for login and session requests. Discovery runs offline with Bun, without downloading the CLI or requiring `npx` on your PATH. If no CLI is available, manually hosted deployments use their API origin for sign-in. Complete the local auth approval shown in the browser when prompted. The runtime API URL stays unchanged. It writes the API URL, the key and the container, not `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL`, so set that one to the same deployment yourself. Once `openbot` exists, the server assigns it as the default by itself unless [Admin → Automatic Learning](docs/automatic-learning.md) has a saved setting. Managed Intelligence needs no separate license token. The same CopilotKit CLI sign-in provisions Composio automatically when you run `bash scripts/start.sh`. If that cannot complete, OpenBot still starts, with apps unavailable. You can run `bun run setup:composio` first to prepare it separately, or later to retry; it does not need a Learning container. The helper creates or reuses one isolated Composio project for this installation and saves its project key to `.env`. Existing Composio keys and Arcade configurations are preserved. Keep the private `.env.openbot-installation-id` file across restarts and interrupted setup attempts; do not copy it into a new installation. This needs a published CopilotKit CLI with `integrations composio provision` and the hosted provisioning service enabled. See [Composio setup](docs/plugins/composio.md#automatic-project-setup) for deployment preparation. 3. Fill the remaining required values: - `OPENAI_API_KEY` Keep the managed Intelligence URLs from `.env.example` unless you run Intelligence yourself. The example `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is public and fine locally; generate your own with: ```sh openssl rand -base64 32 ``` 4. Run: ```sh bash scripts/start.sh ``` 5. Open . `scripts/start.sh` pulls the OpenBot images at the tag in `backend-images.env`, starts Docker services, applies migrations, starts the API server on port 3001 and the routine worker from the OpenBot server image, starts the app from this checkout on port 3010, and checks that the services answer their own health routes before printing next steps. It pulls on every start, so a checkout of `main` runs the images built from main now; offline, it uses the copies already on the machine. The server's log is `docker compose logs server`. `scripts/stop.sh` takes the same things down, including each Bot's computer, which compose does not own; `--keep-computers` leaves the computers running. Nothing is deleted: the database, the Bots' files and their browser profiles are volumes. ### On Windows Run the clone inside WSL 2 with Ubuntu, and run every step above from an Ubuntu terminal. [Windows (WSL 2)](docs/development.md#windows-wsl-2) lists what to install in Ubuntu first. Keep an Ubuntu terminal open while you use OpenBot, and open the app from your Windows browser at . ### Intelligence on your own machine To try Intelligence on one Mac instead of the managed service, follow [Evaluate Intelligence locally](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/intelligence/self-hosting-local). The free [Developer plan](https://www.copilotkit.ai/pricing) qualifies. The local license lasts 30 days and `npx copilotkit@latest local renew` renews it as often as you need, while your account is in good standing. It is a preview for macOS with Docker Desktop, not a production installation. Run its `npx copilotkit@latest local connect` from the OpenBot root, where `.env` is. That command writes `INTELLIGENCE_API_URL`, `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL` and `CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY` to `.env`. OpenBot reads those settings directly; no key copying or renaming is needed. `INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY` remains supported for older configurations. When both are set, the non-empty CLI key takes precedence so reconnecting uses the new project's key. To give the Bots a Learning container on that stack, see [Automatic Learning](docs/automatic-learning.md). ## Deploy it One image carries the app, the API, the browser the Bots drive, and optionally PostgreSQL. Same `.env`, no Kubernetes. ```sh # The published image. Nothing to clone and nothing to build. docker run -p 3001:3001 --env-file .env \ -e EMBEDDED_POSTGRES=on -v openbot-data:/var/lib/postgresql \ ghcr.io/copilotkit/openbot:latest ``` Everything is on 3001 here, the app included, rather than the 3010 the clone uses. `latest` is the most recent release and a version tag such as `:v1.0.1` pins one. Leave `EMBEDDED_POSTGRES` off and set `DATABASE_URL` to point at a database you already run. [docs/deployment.md](docs/deployment.md) has the minimum sizes, the platform notes, and how it behaves behind more than one replica. ## Try it Pick a task you know well enough to review. For example, ask a Bot to check a hotel receipt against a travel policy in Drive. Have it show the room rate and tax separately so you can decide whether the claim meets the nightly limit. Use **Teach a Bot** to record the steps you want it to follow on the next claim. - Open `/bot` and ask: `Open news.ycombinator.com and tell me the top story.` - Ask the Bot to fill out , then inspect `/admin/audit`. - Open `/admin/boundaries`, add a deny rule or preset, and retry the same browser action. - Create a Bot from `/bots`, give it a standing role, and start a channel with it. ## What it is In Personal Edition, you start with one assistant on your computer. With the source template, Docker Compose starts the supporting services, PostgreSQL stores the workspace configuration, and you choose the model. OpenBot encrypts stored model credentials and keeps them out of logs. The team template comes with two Bots. **General Assistant** helps with everyday work. **Knowledge** answers questions from the company documents you connect and cites its sources. To add a Bot, open `/bots` or start from one of the [YAML examples](examples/fintech/catalog/). For example, [Meeting Follow-ups](examples/fintech/catalog/meeting-follow-ups.yaml) reads meeting notes and lists who agreed to do what. Copy its file into `examples/fintech/agents/` and restart OpenBot to try it. You grant tool access separately, so you can let a Bot read a document without giving it permission to edit it. More at [open.bot](https://open.bot). ## Built on AG-UI A Bot is any endpoint speaking [AG-UI](https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui), the open protocol for agent-to-user interaction, so OpenBot is not tied to a framework and neither are you. Agents built with LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK or written by hand all arrive the same way, and the governance rides the protocol rather than the framework. ## Main surfaces A Bot has eight things, always listed in this order: Conversations, Routines, Memory, Skills, Apps, Computer, Approvals and Activity. [How OpenBot works](docs/how-openbot-works.md) explains each one. Each is set in at most three places: for one Bot on its page, for every Bot in the main menu (Routines, Memory, Skills, Connections) or Settings (the rest), and, in the team edition, for everyone in Admin. | | One Bot | Every Bot | Everyone (Admin) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Conversations | `/channel/:id`, `/bot?agent=` | `/`, `/channel/new` | | | Routines | `/bots/:id/routines` | `/routines` | `/admin/proactive` | | Memory | `/bots/:id/memory` | `/memory` | | | Skills | `/bots/:id/skills` | `/skills` | `/admin/skills`, `/admin/learning` | | Apps | `/bots/:id/apps` | `/connections` | `/admin/plugins`, `/admin/components`, `/admin/playground` | | Computer | `/bots/:id/computer` | `/settings/computer` | `/admin/computers` | | Approvals | `/bots/:id/approvals` | `/settings/approvals` | `/admin/approvals`, `/admin/boundaries`, `/admin/what-if` | | Activity | `/bots/:id/activity` | `/settings/activity` (personal edition) | `/admin/audit` | Beside the eight: | Route | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `/bots` | Every Bot you can reach; create one, and open its page to change it. | | `/bots/:id` | One Bot: what it waits on you for, what it is doing, and its rows in the order above. | | `/bots/:id/setup` | The Bot's name, instructions and who it hands work to. | | `/bots/:id/reach`, `/bots/:id/sharing` | Team edition: reach the Bot in Slack, Microsoft Teams or by text, and share it. | | `/settings` | Your account and preferences. | | `/settings/notifications` | Where updates go, your devices, and recent deliveries. | | `/settings/vault` | Your saved logins and, in the personal edition, your keys. No Bot sees what is in it. | | `/settings/setup` | What OpenBot has and still needs. | | `/admin/credentials` | Admin → Vault: write-only encrypted credentials for the deployment. | | `/admin/people`, `/admin/permissions`, `/admin/identity-providers`, `/admin/providers` | Admin → Team: who can sign in, what they may do, and which models Bots use. | Old addresses redirect to the pages above: | Old address | Opens | | --- | --- | | `/capabilities`, `/capabilities/skills`, `/settings/skills`, `/settings/learning` | `/skills` | | `/settings/skills/new`, `/settings/skills/:slug` (personal edition) | `/skills/new`, `/skills/:slug` | | `/capabilities/memory`, `/settings/memory` | `/memory`, which opens `/bots` in the personal edition | | `/responsibilities` | `/routines` | | `/bots/:id/responsibilities` | `/bots/:id/routines` | | `/bots/:id/access` | `/bots/:id/apps` | | `/settings/passwords`, `/settings/credentials` | `/settings/vault` | | `/settings/credentials/new` | `/settings/vault/new` in the personal edition, `/settings/vault` in the team edition | | `/settings/this-computer` | `/settings/computer#this-computer` | | `/settings/browsers` | `/settings/computer#browsers` | ## Features - **A computer per person**: the supervisor gives each person their own container, with a folder and browser profile for each of their Bots. Tick Isolated on a Bot to give it a container of its own. Set `COMPUTER_RUNTIME=runsc` to run them under gVisor where the host supports it. - **A shell, not just a browser**: a Bot can run a command in its workspace, install what it needs, and process a file it saved. Through the same gate as everything else, so a rule can refuse a shell outright or refuse particular commands, and the command is on the record either way. The command inherits PATH, locale, terminal and proxy variables, not the rest of the deployment's environment. - **The gateway is the only way in**: it resolves the target from a server-held snapshot, evaluates the policy, writes the audit row, and only then calls the computer. There is no path that acts without the record existing first. - **CEL policy, fail closed**: rules can inspect `tool.name`, `intent`, `bot.id`, `actor.id`, `page.url`, `page.host`, `element.*`, `key`, `command`, `file.*`, `mcp.*` and `initiator.*` (what started the run, so a rule can refuse a scheduled routine what it would allow a person). Deny is evaluated before allow, a missing policy permits nothing, and a broken rule refuses rather than opens. - **Watch what it is doing**: the screen shows what a Bot is looking at, and the Activity list under it shows what it ran, read and saved in this conversation, with the output. A command line in the transcript opens to the same thing. A saved file shows its path and size, never its contents. - **Take the wheel**: a Bot that hits a login wall or a 2FA prompt asks for help. Control is handed over in the same panel and recorded as `computer.help_requested`, `computer.control_taken` and `computer.control_released`. While a person is driving, Bot actions are refused rather than queued. - **Secrets never enter the transcript**: the trail records that a secret was requested and how long it was, not what it said. - **Bring your own agent**: any AG-UI endpoint is a Bot, on a framework or hand-written. Endpoints are validated with the same target checks used for browser navigation, and an auth header is stored write-only. - **Components instead of prose**: compiled React components live in `app/src/components/gallery/`, sandboxed ones are authored in `/admin/playground` and published with no deployment. Every call asks the server whether the component exists, is published, and is not withheld from that Bot. Data functions are granted per component. - **Governed MCP**: Google Drive, Notion and the [public-web research providers](docs/web-research.md) Parallel, Exa and Firecrawl ship in the catalogue, and Composio brokers a few hundred more apps behind one account (Arcade can be the broker instead), each reached as the person asking. The catalogue carries only vendors this deployment stands behind, so adding one is a review of that vendor. Custom servers must pass URL checks; unknown tools and custom-server tools are treated as writes, and a catalogue tool the server advertises but does not name as a write classifies as a read. A Bot is told which connectors exist here and which it holds, so it says it has not been granted one rather than browsing to the vendor's website. - **Skills are instructions, not capabilities**: personal skills attach only to Bots their author owns, deployment skills are admin-owned, and both are invoked with `/` in the composer. A Bot granted the shipped `skill-creator` skill can write one with you in the conversation, and saves it only when you press the button on the card. - **Sign in with what your company already has**: Google, Microsoft or Okta from the environment, or a company's own SAML or OpenID Connect provider registered while the deployment runs and routed by email domain. Any one turns sign-in on; several may be configured at once. - **Decide who gets in**: `/admin/people` lists everybody who has signed in, promotes and demotes them, and removes access, which ends the session they are using and stops the next sign-in. Every change is on the audit trail. - **An audit trail you can read**: `/admin/audit` lists what was permitted, what was refused and what failed, and every refusal carries the rule that caused it. - **Credentials encrypted at rest**: stored through `/admin/credentials`, never returned by an API, and redacted from audit events. - **Loopback by default**: computers bind to `127.0.0.1` and require a per-container token, so nothing reaches a logged-in browser by knowing its port. The supervisor binds there too, because it holds the Docker socket and its token is a shared secret rather than a network boundary. - **Durable threads and memory**: conversations survive restarts through CopilotKit Intelligence, and each deployment stamps the threads it owns. - **Routines**: ask a Bot to do something on a schedule and it does, running as you, in the channel you asked in. A 15-minute floor and a cap of 20 enabled routines keep a sentence from scheduling more than a person meant, and ten failures in a row switch a routine off rather than burn model spend forever. Needs a worker process, which `scripts/start.sh` starts locally; see [docs/routines.md](docs/routines.md). ## Bring your own agent Any AG-UI endpoint can be a Bot. From `/bots`, create a Bot with: - name and instructions, which become its role description; - private or public visibility; - optional AG-UI endpoint, with the framework the agent is built on when it is one New Bot lists; - optional write-only authorization header. The server validates agent endpoints with the same target checks used for browser navigation, at registration and again on every redirect the endpoint answers with. If no custom endpoint is set, product-created coworkers use `MANAGED_AGENT_AG_UI_URL` when it is configured, and otherwise run in the OpenBot server on their role description. A private address is refused unless it is listed in `AGENT_ENDPOINT_ALLOWED_HOSTS`: ```sh AGENT_ENDPOINT_ALLOWED_HOSTS=agents.internal,10.0.0.42:9000 ``` A host on its own covers any port on that host; a host with a port pins that port. Matching is exact: no wildcards, no suffixes. An entry written as a URL, or containing `*`, stops startup and names that entry. The list covers agent endpoints only. Browsing is unaffected, the addresses holding a deployment's own cloud credentials are refused whatever is listed, and listing an address permits registering an agent there rather than granting that agent anything. Tenant package agents are declared in the package's own `agents.yaml`, in the directory `TENANT_PACKAGE_DIR` names (`examples/fintech` by default), or each in a file of its own under that package's `agents/` directory, as one of: - `built-in`, with a system prompt; - `remote-ag-ui`, with an endpoint; or - `remote-mastra`, with a Mastra server's address. See [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md) and [docs/coworkers.md](docs/coworkers.md). ## Configuration `.env.example` is the source template. The API server refuses to start without: - `DATABASE_URL` - `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` - `INTELLIGENCE_API_URL` - `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL` - `CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY` (or the older `INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY`) `COPILOTKIT_LICENSE_TOKEN` is optional. A self-hosted Intelligence with its own license can still set it and it is forwarded to the runtime; managed Intelligence does not issue one and startup no longer asks for it. A self-hosted Intelligence also needs the license on its own deployment, or it refuses memory; OpenBot logs `intelligence-entitlement-not-ready` at boot when that is missing. Settings worth knowing: | Variable | Use | | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER` | Admits every request as one administrator. Required when no identity provider is configured; `.env.example` ships it on. | | `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | Answers the OpenAI-shaped calls from somewhere else: a gateway, a proxy. | | `COPILOTKIT_OPENAI_API` | `responses` or `chat`: the OpenAI API the built-in Bots call behind that `OPENAI_BASE_URL`. Unset, models that take tools only through the Responses API (`gpt-5.6` and later) get `responses` and the rest get `chat`. | | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `GOOGLE_GENERATIVE_AI_BASE_URL` | The same, for those two APIs. | | `COMPUTER_TOKEN` | Secret every Bot computer request must present. `start.sh` falls back to a fixed dev value. | | `SUPERVISOR_TOKEN` | Secret the supervisor requires. `start.sh` falls back to a fixed dev value. | | `AGENT_TOOL_TOKEN` | Secret a Bot presents to call a granted tool back. `start.sh` sets one. Without it no Bot may call tools. | | `COMPUTER_SUPERVISOR_URL` | Gives each person a computer of their own instead of one shared computer. | | `COMPUTER_RUNTIME` | Set to `runsc` to run computers under gVisor, where the host has it. | | `COMPUTER_SANDBOX` | Set to `on` for Chromium's own sandbox, where the host permits it. | | `EMBEDDED_POSTGRES` | Set to `on` for a database inside the deployment container. | | `AGENT_COMPUTER_POLICY` | JSON action policy. Malformed JSON stops server startup. | | `AGENT_COMPUTER_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS` | Lets a Bot reach this machine's own services. It never shows on a paid Intelligence plan. | Full reference: [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md). ## Services and ports | Service | Port | Purpose | | ------------------------ | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `app` | 3010 | React/Vite UI. | | `server` | 3001 | Hono API, CopilotKit runtime, auth, policy, audit, plugins, components, coworkers, and channels. | | `agent-computer` | 4100 | Chromium plus `/workspace` and browser profile. | | `agent-bot` | 4200 | Proof-of-concept AG-UI Bot. | | `agent-langgraph` | 4201 | LangGraph AG-UI Bot. | | `agent-harness` | 4202 to 4214, per framework | The agent framework picked in OpenBot Desktop setup, behind the `harness` Compose profile. | | `supervisor` | 4500 host / 4300 container | Creates and manages one computer per person, and one per Isolated Bot. | | `worker` | none | Fires due routines by handing each run to the server. | | PostgreSQL | 5432 | Product data, policy, audit, credentials, grants, channels, and component metadata. | | CopilotKit Intelligence | external | Durable threads and memory. | The server gateway is the product/API path for Bot browser and file tool calls. It resolves the target, evaluates policy, writes an audit row, and then calls `agent-computer`. The computer also exposes lower-level token-protected service endpoints; keep them private and do not use them to bypass the gateway. More detail: [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md). ## Sign in `.env.example` ships `OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true`, which is one administrator and no sign-in: how a fresh clone reaches the product without registering an OAuth client first. Delete that line and configure **any one** of Google, Microsoft or Okta before anybody else can reach the deployment. With neither, it refuses to start rather than admitting everybody as an administrator. Configure more than one provider and the sign-in screen offers each of them. These four are needed whichever you pick: ```sh BETTER_AUTH_URL=http://localhost:3001 # where OAuth callbacks come back to BETTER_AUTH_SECRET= # openssl rand -base64 32 TRUSTED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:3010 # where the app is served from INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS=you@example.com # comma separated ``` Then the provider. Register the redirect URI shown beside it. ```sh # Google — http://localhost:3001/api/auth/callback/google GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID= GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET= # Microsoft — http://localhost:3001/api/auth/callback/microsoft MICROSOFT_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID= MICROSOFT_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET= MICROSOFT_OAUTH_TENANT_ID=common # your directory GUID for staff only # Okta — http://localhost:3001/api/auth/callback/okta OKTA_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID= OKTA_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET= OKTA_OAUTH_ISSUER=https://example.okta.com/oauth2/default ``` Restart. Accounts, sessions and roles are stored in the same PostgreSQL database as everything else. A company's own SAML or OpenID Connect provider is registered while the deployment runs, under Admin → Identity providers, and routed by email domain. An OIDC registration needs every host in the provider's discovery document listed in `TRUSTED_ORIGINS`, not only the issuer. - `INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS` is required, because it is what grants the first administrator. After that `/admin/people` can promote others, but an address named here stays an administrator and cannot be demoted or removed from that screen. It is re-read on every sign-in, so editing it takes effect the next time that person signs in. - `MICROSOFT_OAUTH_TENANT_ID` defaults to `common`, which admits personal Microsoft accounts as well as work ones. On a multi-tenant app registration Entra may send no `email` claim at all, so OpenBot falls back to `upn` and then `preferred_username`. If none of the three arrives the sign-in is refused and the reason is logged: add `email` as an optional claim, or use your directory GUID here. - A half-configured provider is refused at start-up rather than at somebody's first attempt to sign in: a client id with no secret, a `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` shorter than 32 characters, or an Okta issuer with no credentials behind it. - **SAML and OIDC** are registered while the deployment runs rather than configured here. Sign in as an administrator and go to Admin → Identity providers with the metadata your identity team gave you. People then sign in by typing their email address, and the domain decides which provider they are sent to. - **Put TLS in front of any deployment.** A page served over plain `http://` on anything but localhost is not a secure context, and sign-in cookies want `Secure`. ### Organization sign-in through another OpenBot A team deployment can leave sign-in to another OpenBot, the authority, configured with the Google, Microsoft or Okta settings above (your Kubernetes OpenBot can serve this role). Set `OPENBOT_ORGANIZATION_AUTH_URL=https://openbot.company.example` to the authority's origin. Use an HTTPS origin; HTTP is accepted only on loopback for local tests. Provider client secrets stay on that authority. The authority verifies the person and their current role; organization mode never substitutes `dev@openbot.local`, and it decides sign-in ahead of `OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER`. This optional URL is separate from `INTELLIGENCE_API_URL`, `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL` and `CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY`. Each deployment keeps its own Intelligence project credential. OpenBot Desktop does not offer organization sign-in. It installs the personal edition, which refuses `OPENBOT_ORGANIZATION_AUTH_URL`, and removes that setting from its `.env` on every Start. ## Keeping it to your machine - `agent-computer` drives a browser holding real logins. `docker-compose.yml` binds it to loopback; leave it there. - Store credentials through `/admin/credentials`, which encrypts them. Do not put credential values in tenant YAML or in committed files. - `AGENT_COMPUTER_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS` lets a Bot reach services on this machine. It ships commented out in `.env.example`, is for a laptop only, and a deployment running with `NODE_ENV=production` refuses to start while it is set. - To reach an agent on your own network from a deployment, list its address in `AGENT_ENDPOINT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` instead. That permits the one address, where the switch above permits the network. ## Development ```sh bun run format:check bun run lint bun run typecheck bun run test bun run build ``` After changing the Drizzle schema: ```sh bun run --filter server db:generate bun run --filter server db:migrate ``` Use `bash scripts/start.sh` for the whole stack and `bash scripts/stop.sh` to take it down.
